subject: physics
question_text: Can the resultant of two vectors of unequal magnitude be zero? Give the reason.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The answer
lines: Two vectors add to zero only when they
are equal in magnitude and opposite in
steps.why: Zero means the two arrows must close on themselves, and only equal-and-opposite arrows do that.
common_mistakes: Answering "yes, if the angle is 180°" — opposite direction alone is not enough.

recall.must_convey: That the answer is no, because cancelling needs equal magnitudes and opposite directions.
reject: mod P minus Q is never zero

steps.label: The reason
lines: The smallest resultant of P and Q is |P − Q|.
Three unequal vectors CAN give zero, if
steps.why: Naming the smallest possible resultant turns a memorised "no" into a proof, and the three-vector line shows exactly where the limit stops.
common_mistakes: Extending the "no" to three vectors — three unequal vectors can close a triangle.

recall.must_convey: That the smallest resultant is mod P minus Q, which is not zero when P is not equal to Q.
accept: smallest is mod P minus Q
not zero when they are unequal
